raw_research: OVERVIEW: Cassidy is an unincorporated community straddling Haslam Creek near the east coast of southern Vancouver Island, British Columbia, on BC Highway 19 about 98 km by road north-west of Victoria and 14 km south of Nanaimo [W][31]. The area is served by the Island Highway, the Island Rail Corridor and the Nanaimo Airport [W]. CURRENT POPULATION (sources conflict): one source lists Cassidy as a hamlet with 971 residents [37], while another describes it as a small rural community with a population just greater than one thousand residents [21][59]. NAME AND FIRST SETTLER: Thomas Cassidy farmed in the Oyster district from the 1870s, and his homestead was called Cassidy's place or Tom Cassidy's [W]. In 1884 his initial 24-hectare (60-acre) preemption was converted into a Crown grant [W]. During railway construction from 1884 to 1886 he supplied the camps near the Nanaimo River with milk and vegetables [W][41]. By the early 1900s the locality was known as Cassidy's Siding [W]. His son, Thomas William Cassidy, sold 211 hectares (522 acres) to the Department of National Defence in 1942 for a Royal Canadian Air Force glider pilot training facility, and the site is now home to the Nanaimo Airport [W]. FOUNDING OF THE COMPANY TOWN (dates conflict): The Granby Consolidated Mining, Smelting and Power Company built the town, also called Granby, for 500 miners and their families [1][13][39]. Sources give different founding years: 1917 [7][3][22], 1918 [39], and 1919 [W]. Granby acquired the Cassidy Coal Company in 1917 and operated the Granby No. 1 Colliery until 1932 [4][14]. Production started in 1918, when the company began working the Douglas coal seam [W][12]. The mine was built to extract a section of the Upper Douglas coal seam originally discovered in 1852 on the Nanaimo River [7]. WHY IT WAS BUILT: The operation was begun to produce coking coal for Granby's copper smelter at Anyox [3][22]. Granby operated B.C.'s two largest copper smelters and the second-largest copper mine in the British Empire [2]. A large proportion of washed coal was shipped to the company's smelter at Anyox for conversion to metallurgical coke [53]. Granby aimed to avoid the disruptive labour unrest of the era by keeping its workforce happy with the best-equipped, most modern mine and living quarters [9]. THE MODEL TOWN: The model town included 19 houses of various sizes connected to power, water and sewer, with provision for a further 50 residences [W]. Another source says the township was designed for 50 houses with running water, lawns, gardens and boulevards, on-site electricity and arc-lighted paved streets [10]. A Vancouver engineering firm was commissioned to design a picture-book townsite of bungalows with electricity and proper sewage disposal [43]. Its tree-lined streets had grass verges and sidewalks [W]. A concrete single men's dormitory with 76 rooms had light, hot and cold water and steam heat, and the mess house had all modern conveniences [W][42]. The town had paved streets, a department store, a theatre and a recreation ground [W]. One source adds a non-denominational church used on demand, and a post office [44]. Miners had steam-heated lockers for their clean clothes [46]. Mine buildings were made of concrete or grey stucco rather than the usual unpainted frame construction [45]. The town sat on a gravelly bench between Haslam Creek and the Nanaimo River [54]. One source calls it 'the best company town in Canada', and says that when jobs went begging elsewhere there was always a waiting list at Granby [49]. Sources give different areas: the town covered 40 hectares (100 acres) [W]; 85 acres north of Haslam Creek and south of the Nanaimo River were allocated for the community [8]; and the townsite and mine workings together covered almost 100 acres [44]. THE MINE: The sandy overburden made mining difficult [W]. At peak production in 1921 and 1922, 450 men worked each shift [W]. In 1928 the mine had 500 employees, with 200 working each eight-hour shift and producing 1,000 tons [W][51]. Another source puts peak output at about 1 million kilograms of coking-quality coal per eight-hour shift [12]. The seam dipped an average of 18 degrees and varied from 1 to 25 ft thick, averaging about 8 ft [24]. Outbursts of gas and coal occurred before 1921, and the first complete record was made on June 14 of that year [25]. The mine was notorious for being extremely wet and for gassy 'blowouts' and 'bumps' [50]. Because the seam was crushed in one section, less than 20% of the coal mined was sold in lump form [52]. Coal travelled on a 4.8 km (3 mi) spur line to the E&N Railway and then by rail to Ladysmith [W]. The spur ran from Cassidy Siding, near today's Country Kitchen restaurant [17]. Seven different mines operated in the vicinity from 1917 to 1953, producing over 2.5 million tonnes of coal [W]. COLLAPSE: The Granby mine closed in 1932 because the coal seam was exhausted, oil was rising in popularity, the mine was dangerous, and the Great Depression had hit [W][19]. When the owners shut down their Anyox smelter during the Depression, Granby was also doomed [18]. Residents abandoned their houses after the closure [W]. For several years the vacant townsite was guarded by a single watchman, Bill John's father [57]. In March 1936 the remnants of the town were auctioned off and largely removed [W][20][27]. By 1951 only a caretaker and skeletal concrete structures remained [W]. Crumbling concrete and fading photographs are about all that is left of Granby [58]. THE RAILWAY: The Cassidy train station opened in 1919 [W]. It was a flag stop when Via Rail service on Vancouver Island ceased in 2011 [W]. In its final years not even a signpost marked the flag stop location, just south of Vowels Rd [W]. THE CASSIDY INN: The building was erected in 1914 as a bunkhouse for Dunsmuir coal surveyors and engineers [W][16]. It became a community recreation centre with a small store run by Napoleon Manca [W][56]. A liquor (beer parlour) licence followed in 1925 [W][28]. The 1953 paving of the Island Highway boosted business [W]. In January 1983 owners Jane and Bob Kelly revived it as a neighbourhood pub [W][29]. In 2013 the building stood in for an Alaskan bar in the Superman film Man of Steel [W]. It closed about 2014 [W]. A fire gutted the vacant building in 2016, on the evening of July 4 [W][30]. WHAT KEEPS PEOPLE THERE TODAY: Logging revived the community through the 1940s and 1950s [W]. The Cassidy Drive-In operated from 1954 to 1992 [W]. The Ray Collishaw Air Terminal, which serves Nanaimo, has been significantly developed since the 1970s [W]. Nanaimo Airport (YCD) is a small privately owned airport at Cassidy [34]. Its administration is at 3238 Mustang Rd [32]. Distances to Nanaimo differ by source: one gives the airport as about 18 km south of downtown Nanaimo [33], another as 14 km [34]. The residential area is a bedroom community for Nanaimo [W]. Commercial businesses line the highway [W]. Nearby are the Rondalyn Resort (camping, RV park and golf course) and Birds Nest Campground, both on Haslam Creek [W]. At Beck Rd there is parking, a picnic area and the Cassidy Country Kitchen [W]. NOTABLE PERSON: Downhill mountain biker Steven Smith (1989–2016) [W].

raw_research:
OVERVIEW: Blacks Harbour is a former village on a harbour of the same name opening onto the Bay of Fundy, and since 1 January 2023 it has been part of the rural community of Eastern Charlotte, New Brunswick, Canada [W]. Locals call it simply "Blacks" [54]. For much of its history it was a company town dependent on the fish processing company Connors Brothers Limited [W][9]. One source says the village exists almost entirely because of the growth of Connors Brothers Limited [9]. The company owned the land, the houses, the stores and most of the jobs [W][8][48].

POPULATION: The 2021 Canadian census counted 907 people living in 385 of 421 private dwellings, up 1.5% from 894 in 2016, on 9.02 km2 [W]. Other sources describe a population of about 900 [39][58]. Historical figures conflict. A 1951 Maclean's article called it a town of two thousand people [35]. Another source called it a prosperous community of 1,200 people [47]. A third says it has only briefly surpassed 1,000 residents [57]. Earlier counts were 100 in 1871, 150 in 1898 and 200 in 1904 [W].

EARLY SETTLEMENT AND NAME: Beginning in the 1780s, 15 land grants were made in the area [W]. In 1866 there was a fishing settlement of about 14 families [W][53]. The local heritage museum dates the village's establishment to 1866 [14][23]. One local history says permanent settlement came only after Patrick and Lewis Connors created the herring industry in the late 1880s [20]. Sources conflict on the name. One says it comes from the Black family, who played a pivotal role in settling the area [22]. A local history says the name was not from the Black family, who settled around 1850, and that the origin is still undiscovered [19][21].

FOUNDING OF THE INDUSTRY: Wikipedia says Irish-born fisherman James Connors and his sons Lewis and Patrick bought land at Blacks Harbour and built a wharf and fish houses [W]. A local history credits Lewis Connors with buying the land [3][24]. The family owned fishing weirs and boats and sold salted and frozen herring and other fish in Canadian and American markets [W]. One source says they built a weir to exploit the large stocks of sardine-sized herring in the clear, cool waters [2]. In 1885 the brothers started a canning business [W][1][3][24]. The following year they built a store for their growing workforce [W]. Their first products were clams, scallops, clam chowder and berries [W][3]. The berries included strawberries, raspberries and blueberries [27]. They began canning sardines in 1889 [W]. That year they put up a few hundred tins [25]. They brought canning equipment from Eastport, Maine, and canned sardines in cottonseed oil [4]. In 1893 the business was incorporated as Connors Bros. Ltd. [W][5]. Sources conflict on the founding date. Several give 1893 as the founding year [15][16][26]. Another says the company was founded in 1885 [59].

COMPANY TOWN LIFE: Workers could buy goods on credit at the company store, with the amount owed deducted from their wages [W]. Lewis Connors built company-owned houses for imported workers [6]. The company also ran a farm that supplied produce, beef and milk to workers [50]. In the 1910s and 1920s Connors Bros paid for school buildings, the post office, a general store, a mill, a dairy farm, a beef farm, a hotel and a baseball field [49]. The company built the first school in 1912 [W]. Electricity arrived in 1928, when Connors Bros. bought power from the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission [W]. A local history describes the result as a self-sustaining community [7].

OWNERSHIP CHANGES: In the early 1920s, conflict between the families of Patrick and Lewis Connors affected management of the company [11]. In 1923 the brothers sold the company to Alan and Neil McLean [12]. At that time the town had few residents and employees were mainly seasonal [29]. The cannery operated only in summer, and its transient workers "camped out" in tents and tarpaper shanties [30]. The McLeans bought can-making and box-making machinery to provide winter employment [32]. They also built homes, schools, hospitals, sporting facilities, water and electric systems and a police department [31]. George Weston Limited bought Connors Bros. in 1967, and Blacks Harbour remained a company town until after that sale [W].

CIVIC INDEPENDENCE: Blacks Harbour was incorporated as a village with an elected mayor and council in 1972 [W]. One source gives the exact date as November 1, 1972 [17]. The village then took over the fire and police departments from the company [W]. Connors Bros. kept control of the water supply, which comes from wells that also serve the plant [W]. In 1982 the company sold its houses, and tenants were given the chance to buy them [W]. In 1992 it sold the village's only building supply store and grocery store [W].

SCALE OF THE SARDINE TRADE: By 1920 the company was producing a million tins a year [28]. In 1950 it packed 490 million sardines into 70 million oblong tins [36]. Even when the retail price of sardines fell to five cents a can, the market stayed strong [34][52]. The company's workforce reached up to 3,600 in the peak canning season [37]. Some processing was still done the traditional way, with workers cutting fish by hand with scissors [55]. New technology was expected to save time and reduce repetitive stress injuries [56]. In 1951 a six-room bungalow in town could be rented for fourteen dollars a month [35].

ECONOMY TODAY: One source describes Connors as the largest employer in town apart from the ferry to Grand Manan [59]. Cooke Aquaculture began about 40 years ago, when Glenn Cooke, his brother and his father started a salmon farm in Blacks Harbour [38]. Its salmon business is the largest division and is still run from the village, although the head office is now in Saint John [39][40]. Cooke employs nearly 1,000 people in Charlotte County [41]. It has 15,000 employees in 15 countries and $4-billion in annual revenue [42]. Tourism New Brunswick lists the Bay of Fundy, Connors Bros., Clover Leaf Seafoods and Cooke Aquaculture as part of the community's identity [43].

FERRY: Blacks Harbour is the northern terminus of the year-round ferry to Grand Manan, operated by Coastal Transport [W][61]. The service began on 30 May 1966; before that, the crossing left from Saint Andrews [W]. The vessels are the Grand Manan Adventure, which runs year-round, and the M.S. Grand Manan V, which runs from late June to early September [61]. Boarding on the mainland is free, and tickets are bought on leaving the island [63]. Frommers lists round-trip fares of C$13 per adult and C$39.25 per car [62]. During one ferry breakdown, more than 300 people, over 10% of Grand Manan's population, were stranded on the mainland [66]. Many visitors are only passing through to catch the ferry [68].

DETAILS: In 1968 a federal building was built for the fisheries department and the post office [W]. In front of it stands a fishermen's monument by New Brunswick sculptor Claude Roussel [W]. Made of iron rods soldered together, it depicts two fishermen and a net, stands over seven feet tall and is painted black [W]. The Connor Bros Nature Preserve covers 106 acres [68]. The village looks out on the Bay of Fundy's tides [54], which one source calls the highest in the world [69].

WHERE AND WHAT: Valka (German: Walk; Estonian: Valga) is a town and the centre of Valka Municipality in Latvia's Vidzeme region, lying on the border with Estonia along both banks of the river Pedele [W]. It is twinned with the Estonian town of Valga, from which it is separated by the national border, and the two use the slogan "One Town, Two Countries" [W].

FOUNDING AND EARLY HISTORY: The town was first mentioned in 1286 [W][1][2][3][4]. That mention appears in Riga's debt book (credit register) [1][2][3]. The 1286 records name Johannes Clericus de Walcot and Johannes Stedinc de Walkot [2]. One source says the 1286 record names the town under the German name WALK [1]. Two others say it was then called Pedele, after the Pedele river [3][4]. By the 14th century the town was already called Valka (Walk in German) [4]. The word "valks" originally described a place where people dragged their boats or cargo from the basin of the River Gauja to the River Pedele [5]. From 1419 the town was the seat of the Landtag of the Livonian Confederation [W]. Walk, an unfortified settlement in the heart of Old Livonia, was chosen 36 times as the location for assembly days [6]. Valka is described as the only ancient city of Latvia where the Knights of the Teutonic Order did not build a castle [7]. The Livonian War (1558-1583) destroyed the city [10]. Stefan Batory, King of Poland, granted city rights in 1584 [W][8]. One source gives the exact date as 11 June 1584 [8]. Since 1994, Valga City Days have been celebrated annually around 11 June, described as the town's founding date [9].

RAILWAY BOOM: The town only gained importance at the end of the 19th century [W]. Two developments drove this: the Vidzeme teacher's seminary operated there, and an important railway junction was developed [W][11]. The seminary was founded by pedagogue Jānis Cimze (1814–1881) and is described as the first higher-education institution in Latvia's territory [W]. The first narrow-gauge railway line in modern Latvia's territory ran from Valka to the Estonian city of Pärnu [W]. The Valga-Riga railway was completed, and in 1889 a connection to Pskov was established [23]. A period quotation says many tradesmen wanted to move there because four railway lines would cross there [12]. Another source counts five railway branches (Riga, Tartu, Pskov, Pärnu and Aluksne), making Valga the second-largest railway junction in Estonia after Tallinn [24]. More than 1,500 people then worked in railway-related businesses [25]. Population rose from 4,200 in 1881 to over 20,000 by the end of World War I [26].

BIRTHPLACE OF LATVIA AND DIVISION: On 15 November 1917, the decision to proclaim the independent Republic of Latvia was made in Valka [W][22]. Latvia's red-white-red flag was raised there for the first time [W]. The town was disputed between the new Latvian and Estonian states [W]. Its population was split nearly evenly between Estonians and Latvians [13]. When Estonian military authorities forcibly evacuated Latvian institutions from Valga, Latvians threatened military measures in response [15]. An international commission headed by British Colonel Stephen George Tallents drew the border [W][17][27]. Sources give 1 July 1920 as the date of division [W][27], while the Estonian foreign ministry timeline dates Tallents's border decision to 3 July 1920 [17]. The line was drawn along a small stream running through the centre of the town [51]. The main part of the town went to Estonia [19][20][28]. This included the railway station and most of the centre [28]. The suburbs of Lugazi and Putraskalns went to Latvia [20]. In return, most of the disputed mixed-population parishes went to Latvia [19]. Neither country was satisfied with the decision [21]. With minor changes, the Tallents line remains the basis of the border today [18].

SOVIET ERA: The town became an important industrial centre with a large Soviet army military base [29]. During the Cuban missile crisis, key Soviet military personnel in charge of rockets were based in Valka [30].

OPEN BORDER: Border controls were abolished in 2007 with Schengen expansion [W][49]. All crossing points were removed, and roads and fences were opened [W]. As of 2025, city bus number 3, run by the Estonian company ATG Bussiliinid OÜ, links the twin towns three times a day from Valga train station [W]. A new bridge over the Varžupīte/Konnaoja river has a swing in the middle, so you can sway between the two countries [52]. A shared central square opened in 2020 [53]. An Orthodox church was built in 2003–05 on the site of an ordinary house that residents had converted into a church after the 1991 border separated them from their only Orthodox church [67].

ECONOMIC ENGINE AND PRESSURES: Valka sits on the A3 state road, where transit and tourist traffic grows every year [32]. Valka has become a popular destination for shopping and services among Estonians, Finns and other tourists [33]. In the other direction, Latvians frequently cross to use the wider range of shops on the Estonian side [38]. Hundreds of Latvians cross to shop every weekend [54]. Forests cover 58.57% of the county's rural territory, which underpins forestry and woodworking [34]. The cross-border labour market is quite active [35]. Wages are higher and the economy stronger in Estonia [W][36]. Latvian textile worker Marite Runka put it this way: "in Valga, you can still find a job" [37][58]. Salaries in the border town are among the lowest in the country [59]. Statistics Estonia, as cited, reports average monthly gross income in "Valka municipality" about 20% below the Estonian average [47]. Many Valka residents have registered as inhabitants of Valga [W]. Roughly 1,000 Latvians are registered in Valga Municipality [39]. A real estate agent, Hans Heinjärv, says one apartment in five in Valga is bought by a Latvian [55]. In one year, 300 Latvians received treatment on the Estonian side and 82 were born there [56]. Valka Municipality, population 8,000 and the smallest municipality in Latvia, had accumulated more than half a million euros in debt by the end of September [40]. Both towns are depopulating and ageing [64]. Habits of separation persist, including different schools, languages and daily routines [61][62]. A project aimed to raise the share of residents who see Valga–Valka as a joint town from 21% [63]. Valka has one primary school and a gymnasium, and the Institute of Latvia-Estonia provides further education [W].

POPULATION (sources conflict): Valka's population was 5,535 on 1 July 2015 [41]. Another source counts 4,718 residents in 2018 [65]. Other figures given are about 4,000 [42], 4,560 [43] and 6,000 [44]. The combined twin town has been put at about 19,000 [45], fewer than 20,000 [46], and 17,170 in 2018 [65].

raw_research:
WHY PEOPLE LIVE HERE: Kili's residents did not choose it freely; the island was settled as a relocation site for the people of Bikini Atoll after Bikini was used for U.S. nuclear testing [W][4][23]. One source states that the Bikinians did not move there on their own and were put there by the US Government [23]. Wikipedia notes the move is sometimes considered a forced relocation [W].

GEOGRAPHY AND BASICS: Kili is a single small island of 81 hectares (200 acres, 0.93 sq km) in the Marshall Islands [W][4]. Another source describes it as one-third of a square mile in land area with no lagoon [56]. It lies about 48 km (30 mi) southwest of Jaluit and belongs to the Ralik Chain legislative district [W]. Unlike Bikini, it has no natural lagoon [W][56]. It is about 1/6 the size of Bikini Atoll [W]. Its highest point is only 3 meters (9.8 ft) above sea level [W].

EARLY HISTORY: Captain Thomas Dennet of the British vessel Britannia sighted the island in 1797, en route from Australia to China, and named it Hunter Island [W]. The German Empire claimed it in 1885 [W]. After World War I it came under Japan's South Seas Mandate, and after World War II it came under U.S. control as part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands [W]. Kili was uninhabited before 1948 [W][3]. It was U.S. government property [3], owned by the U.S. Trust Territory government [4].

FOUNDING — THE BIKINI EXODUS: Wikipedia says the Bikini islanders agreed in 1945 to let the U.S. temporarily use Bikini for nuclear testing, which they were told was of great importance to humankind [W]. Other sources place the key events in 1946: in February 1946 Commodore Ben H. Wyatt, military governor of the Marshalls, traveled to Bikini and assembled the people after church [5]. In 1946 Bikini became the site of Operation Crossroads [2]. The islanders were told they could return home after the tests were completed [W][7]. There were no words in Marshallese for nuclear weapons, radiation or fallout [6].

On March 7 (1946), weeping and singing farewells, 167 Bikini people were transported to Rongerik [8]. Britannica gives the figure as 166 and says they were relocated to Rongerik and Kili in 1946 [29]. Rongerik's resources had been greatly exaggerated to them [9]. Food ran out, and the Bikinians suffered starvation and fish poisoning [10]. When an official named Mason arrived on January 31, 1948, he found people eating a gruel of flour and water [11]. He judged them to be in "an extreme state of impoverishment" and recommended immediate relocation [12].

In March 1948 they were moved to Kwajalein Atoll [13]. There they lived in tents on a strip of grass beside the airport runway [W][13]. Final choices narrowed to Wotto Atoll, which was populated, and the single island of Kili [14]. Settling on already-inhabited islands was feared to cause social conflicts with residents [20]. In June 1948 the Bikinians chose Kili because it was not ruled by a paramount king, or iroij [W][18]. One account says they wanted political freedom [19]. A 1957 report says the majority allegedly voted for Kili over Wotto [15].

The sources differ on when the advance party went. Two dozen Bikinian men accompanied 8 Seabees to Kili to begin building a village; Wikipedia dates this to June 1948 [W], while Niedenthal dates it to September 1948 [16]. On November 2, 1948 (early November per [15]), 184 Bikinians were moved to Kili [W][15]. It was their third community relocation in two years [17]. Islanders believe Kili was once an ancient burial ground for kings and therefore laden with spiritual influence [27]. The Bikinians have always considered Kili like a prison [32].

The 1957 agreement: the Bikinians, without legal representation, gave the U.S. complete control of Bikini Atoll and gave up future claims [W][30]. In exchange they received $25,000 cash and a $300,000 trust fund paying about $5,000 semi-annually, roughly $15 per person per year [W]. They were also given Kili and several islands in Jaluit Atoll [W].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: There is effectively no self-sustaining economy; life on Kili depends on U.S.-funded compensation and trust funds [W][44][45]. The island cannot produce enough food for self-sufficiency [W][61]. Residents rely on imported food paid for under a settlement agreement with the U.S. government [W]. Imports include USDA rice and canned goods [61]. Spam is among the imported canned foods [62]. Survival on Kili meant dependence on imported food and the rapid loss of a subsistence culture [33]. Trust-fund payments made the Bikinians economically dependent [44]. Diet and lifestyle changes are linked to health problems such as heart disease among Marshallese people [63].

The main agricultural product is copra [W]. However, Kili had little revenue potential from copra or other marketable commodities [34]. Produce, in descending quantity, is coconuts, limes, breadfruit, squash, bananas, papayas and sugar cane [W][67]. A small farm produces melons and some vegetables, but the coral soil is poor [W][68]. Fishing is difficult without a protective lagoon [W]. One account says that for six months of the year you can't fish [31]. Another says that most of the year Kili is surrounded by 10 to 20 foot waves that keep islanders from fishing and sailing canoes [57]. A cold storage facility helps preserve catches [70].

Compensation history: in 1982 the Bikinians received a second trust fund of $20 million, the Resettlement Trust Fund [39]. It was later supplemented with $90 million for cleanup [40]. A KBE source refers to US$90 million given in the early 1990s [52]. A damage payment of $75 million was paid over 15 years at $5 million per year [42]. Of this, $2.4 million is distributed yearly as quarterly per capita payments [43]. A 1994 article said that, without a single industry, the Bikinians found their $2,000 annual stipend woefully inadequate [45]. In 2018 the KBE mayor Anderson Jibas testified hoping Bikini would become a diving and tourism destination again, bringing revenue [55].

2017–2023 COLLAPSE: In 2017 the KBE (Kili/Bikini/Ejit) leaders requested and received full control of the trust fund from the U.S. [W][47]. Sources differ on the fund's size at handover: over $70 million per Wikipedia [W], and $59 million in 2017 per Civil Beat [47]. By early 2023 it was down to $100,000 [W][48]. The result was loan defaults, unpaid wages and halted services [W]. One power-station worker had not been paid in six months, along with 350 other council employees [49]. The fund had supported KBE government operations, including the Kili power plant [46]. The Heine administration declared a state of emergency for Kili [50][73]. The Cabinet identified $200,000 for Kili [51], and a vessel was sent with fuel, food and supplies [74].

SURPRISING FACTS: Ships cannot reach Kili four months of the year because of rough seas [W][59]. The island has neither harbor nor lagoon; a contractor literally surfed equipment ashore [60]. A 40-foot (12 m) copra boat donated in 1949 was washed onto the reef by heavy surf in 1951 [W][35]. It sank while carrying a full load of copra [35]. Typhoon Lola in late 1957 damaged crops and sank the supply ship [66]. Food supplies have run critically low many times because of rough seas and infrequent ships [65][64].

Since 2011 residents have experienced ocean flooding they attribute to global warming [W]. Waves covered parts of the island at least five times from 2011 to 2015, contaminating all wells [W]. In August 2015 the Bikini Council asked the U.S. to allow trust funds to be used to relocate the people again, this time outside the Marshall Islands [W]. When their forefathers left Bikini, they dismantled the church and carried it to Rongerik and each subsequent home [79].

VIVID DETAILS: Each family receives 2–3 shipments a year of 1–2 boxes of frozen chicken, 2–4 50-lb bags of flour, and 2–4 bags of rice [W][69]. Home-based stores sell salt, Tabasco, candy and canned goods [W][68]. Families live in cinder block houses with air-conditioning and electricity [W]. Many prefer to cook outdoors in cook-huts over an open flame [W]. The Bikini Public Works Department oversees imports, maintains houses and runs the power plant [W]. Two Spectra LB-2800 watermakers supply 5,600 gallons per day of drinking water, powered by a solar and wind array [71][72].

The grass Kili Airport is served by Air Marshall Islands [W]. The runway becomes extremely muddy and unusable during and after rain, and has flooded from rising ocean [W]. One resident was flown from Kili to the hospital in Majuro for a severe headache [78].

There are two churches, Assembly of God and Protestant [W]. The Protestant church is a community gathering place [80]. Many Bikinians are buried in a small hilltop cemetery in the middle of the island [81]. Kili Elementary School covers kindergarten through eighth grade, with classes of 6 to 18 students [W]. A mural is painted on the school [82]. Since 2000 the Dartmouth Volunteer Teaching Program has placed 2–4 American teachers there yearly [W]. Eighth graders must pass a test to attend high school in Jaluit or Majuro [W].

POPULATION (sources conflict): 415 people as of 2021, mostly Bikini descendants [W][84]. 548 Bikini people on Kili per the 2020 census [83]. About 800 Bikinians on Kili per LLNL, alongside 2,550 on Majuro, 300 on Ejit, 350 elsewhere in the Marshalls, and about 1,400 abroad [53][54].

raw_research:
Copper Cliff is a community and former company town in Greater Sudbury, Ontario, Canada [W]. It is described as a mining, smelting, and administrative centre that was a company town from 1886 until 1973, when it became part of the City of Sudbury [22]. People live here because of the nickel-copper ore and the smelter built to process it: the community was originally founded as a company town for the nearby Inco (now Vale) nickel smelter [45].

FOUNDING. In 1883, during construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, blacksmith Tom Flanagan discovered chalcopyrite deposits in the area of what is now Copper Cliff [W][2]. One source says Thomas Flanagan, a blacksmith on the CPR, noticed a rust-coloured patch of rock in August of the discovery year [1]. His find was the first local discovery to spur further exploration [5]. The first land purchased for mining was bought by William and Thomas Murray, Henry Abbott and John Laughrin [4]. Samuel J. Ritchie, a capitalist from Akron, Ohio, arrived in 1886 to form the Canadian Copper Company [6][9]. Ritchie's Canadian Copper Company was American-owned and began mining that spring [8]. Sources differ on the founding date: one says Copper Cliff was founded as a company town by the Canadian Copper Company in the 1890s [W], while others say Ritchie founded the company at Copper Cliff in 1886 [9] and that it was a company town from 1886 [22]. One source says the site was named in 1771 by Arctic explorer Samuel Hearne for copper deposits in the area's cliffs [23]; no other source supports this. The ore was first shipped to a smelting plant in Constable Hook, New Jersey, where it was found to be rich in nickel [W]. After the high nickel content was discovered, Ritchie built a nickel smelter at Copper Cliff in 1888 [16]. Robert M. Thompson discovered the first commercially viable method of separating nickel from copper in 1893 [W]. The town was incorporated in 1901, when it had a larger population than the Town of Sudbury [W][20].

ECONOMIC ENGINE. Large-scale nickel mining began in 1902 with the formation of the International Nickel Company, which was backed by J.P. Morgan and Charles Schwab [W]. The Canadian Copper Company became a subsidiary of this New York-headquartered holding company [21]. In 1916 the company was accused of selling metals from Canada to Germany during World War One [W]. It then formed a Canadian subsidiary, the International Nickel Company of Canada (later Inco), incorporated in Copper Cliff in 1916 [W][33]. Copper Cliff Mine, located behind the present police station, was one of the company's mines [7]. Matte was shipped to the United States to be refined [32]. The Copper Cliff Roast Yard operated from 1901 to 1915 [29]. Roasting involved putting raw ore onto layers of cordwood, setting it alight and letting it smoulder for several months [62]. In the old "glory hole", men worked 10- to 14-hour shifts prying ore from the walls with picks, bars and hammers [27]. Vale took over when it purchased Inco in 2007 [40]. Pure nickel metal is produced at Vale's facilities [42]. Copper concentrate is produced at Sudbury and shipped to Noranda for processing [43].

COMPANY CONTROL AND SEGREGATION. The company treated housing and the town as investments and a 'tool' for controlling workers [14]. In 1886, and for many years afterwards, company policy was to provide housing only for Anglo-Saxons [17]. Non-Anglo-Saxons, most of whom worked sporadically as labourers and were considered expendable, were expected to provide their own accommodation in Shantytown, on leased land [12][54]. Immigrant workers such as Poles, Finns, Italians and French Canadians lived in Shantytown, just south of the mine [W]. Sources differ on where managers lived. One says engineers and administrative staff lived in company-planned housing away from the mine [W]. Another says they lived in Sudbury and travelled daily by train to the mine [10]. General manager E. J. Peters stated that the company received 20 per cent interest on small houses being built [52]. Small houses paid a higher return than larger dwellings [53]. In one six-month period, one hundred houses and twelve stores were built [78]. The company leased land for businesses, forbade liquor sales, and allowed leases to transfer only to parties it approved [71][72]. Most councils were acclaimed rather than elected [70][69]. The town's police were on Inco's payroll [69]. Excluded union men left the district, and the remaining workforce avoided union organization until the 1940s [19]. By the end of World War II the Mine Mill and Smelter Workers Union had gained recognition [37]. During the Depression, one source says, the only way to get a job was to strengthen one of the mines' hockey or soccer teams [74].

SURPRISING / VIVID DETAILS. The early town was described as stark and ugly, with vegetation devastated by sulphur fumes [58]. Pigs, cows and dogs roamed freely through the dusty streets [59]. Typhoid fever was ever present [60]. In 1910, seven Ukrainian families on Elizabeth Street lodged eighty-six single men [57]. Before 1898 there was no resident doctor; Dr. Struthers came from Sudbury every other day [91]. A blackboard listed the names of people who wanted a visit from the doctor [92]. Sources differ on the hospital's date: one says the company-run hospital came in 1900 [66], while another says the first hospital was built in 1902 and destroyed by fire in 1912 [94]. The Copper Cliff Hospital operated for 73 years, and its medical staff pioneered industrial medicine [93]. A community centre with northern Ontario's first indoor swimming pool opened in 1915 [66]. The Copper Cliff Club opened May 5, 1916, at a cost of $80,000 [67]. Copper Cliff Dairy was founded in 1927 by four Finnish immigrant families [85]. Son John Edward delivered its milk house to house in personalized bottles, beginning at age 13 [86]. In 1929 the company bought a snow plow nicknamed "Big Bertha" [89]. Inco ran picnics, regattas and ski meets [75]. The sintering plant, which ran from 1948 to 1963, produced nickel sulphide and sulphur dioxide linked to respiratory cancers among workers [W]. On June 10, 1956, Jean Gagnon and coworkers staged a wildcat strike that blocked entry to the smelter for a day [W]. Afterward, 90% of men always wore masks in the plant [W]. The Inco Superstack was completed in 1972 under pressure from the community and province to disperse emissions [W]. It was the world's tallest chimney until 1987 and was decommissioned in 2020 [W]. It measures 381 m (1,250 ft) high, 35 m wide at the base and 16 m at the top [39]. Outsiders see the stack as a symbol of pollution, but locals see it as a symbol of workers' identity, evoking "smokestack nostalgia" [W]. Little Italy grew near the base of the Superstack, around Diorite and Craig Streets [W]. Many of its families trace their roots to Metaurilia, near Fano [W]. Italian-language stores and services made it unnecessary for residents to visit the non-Italian parts of Copper Cliff [W][83]. When Italy entered the Second World War on June 10, 1940, several hundred Italian Canadians in Sudbury were interned as "enemy aliens" [W]. One local store nearly went bankrupt extending credit to the wives of men who were jobless or interned [84].

ANNEXATION AND POPULATION. Sudbury repeatedly tried to annex Copper Cliff to tax its mining facilities [W]. It succeeded in 1973, when about 4,000 people lived there [W]. Residents held a ceremony on 31 December 1972 to mourn the town [W]. Sources differ on the current population: one gives 2,007 [49], and another gives 2,124 for 2020 [50]. The same source gives the area as 1.726 km² [49]. Greater Sudbury had 166,004 people in the 2021 census [51].

raw_research:
OVERVIEW: St Kilda (Scottish Gaelic: Hiort) is a remote archipelago 35 nautical miles (65 km) west-northwest of North Uist in the North Atlantic, containing the westernmost islands of the Outer Hebrides of Scotland [W]. One source describes it as lying more than 40 miles west of the Outer Hebrides, and another as 110 miles off Scotland's coast [88][89]. The largest island is Hirta, and Dùn, Soay and Boreray were also used for grazing and seabird hunting [W]. The archipelago is owned by the National Trust for Scotland [W].

CURRENT POPULATION: There are no permanent residents today [W][37][40]. Hirta is occupied year-round by people working at the Ministry of Defence base [W][37]. Wikipedia says the island population varies between 20 and 70, most living there temporarily, including MOD employees, National Trust for Scotland employees and scientists on a Soay sheep research project [W]. Wikitravel gives a total population 'well under 50' [43]. National Trust for Scotland staff are resident from April to October each year [38].

FOUNDING AND EARLY SETTLEMENT: Sources differ on how long people have lived here. Wikipedia says St Kilda was continuously inhabited for two millennia or more, from the Bronze Age until 1930 [W]. A UNESCO document says Hirta has been occupied almost continuously for well over 2,000 years [8]. The National Trust for Scotland is quoted as saying a community existed for at least 4,000 years [6]. Visit Outer Hebrides is quoted as saying the islands were originally settled between four and five thousand years ago [7]. In 2015 the first direct evidence of Neolithic settlement emerged: sherds of Hebridean-ware pottery found east of the village [W]. A stone-tool quarry on Mullach Sgar above Village Bay was also found, and one source says it was worked over 5,000 years ago [W][5]. The pottery appears to be made of local material, suggesting settlement in the 4th millennium BC [W]. Archaeologist Alan Hunter Blair reported intensive Iron Age occupation at the eastern end of Village Bay [W][3]. Finds of brooches, an iron sword and Danish coins, along with Norse place names, indicate a sustained Viking presence [W][12]. One source says the Vikings may have settled the islands [10]. Another says they used St Kilda as a base for hunting and fishing expeditions [11]. The first written record may date from 1202, when an Icelandic cleric wrote of sheltering on 'the islands that are called Hirtir' [W][18]. The islands were historically part of the domain of the MacLeods of Harris, whose steward collected rents in kind [W]. One source says the Macleods of Dunvegan took control in the 14th century [21]. Another says the islands were owned by the MacLeods of Harris and Dunvegan [22]. When Martin Martin visited in 1697 the population was about 180 [W][23]. Population probably never exceeded 180 [W]. In 1727 disease killed so many that too few remained to man the boats, and new families were brought in from Harris [W]. In 1852, 36 islanders emigrated to Australia on the Priscilla, reducing the population to 70 [W]. Eighteen of those 36 died of sickness on the ship or in quarantine [W].

NAME: No saint named Kilda ever existed [W][19]. The name first appears in a 1592 pilot book by Lucas Waghenaer [W]. One theory derives it from Tobar Childa, a well on Hirta [W][20].

ECONOMIC ENGINE (HISTORIC): The mainstay of the islanders' food supply was seabirds, especially gannet and fulmar, harvested as eggs and young birds and eaten fresh and cured [W]. The birds provided meat, oil, eggs and feathers [27][34]. UNESCO describes a subsistence economy based on birds, agriculture and sheep farming [25]. It also notes reliance on seabird products as the main source of livelihood [26]. The islanders kept up to 2,000 sheep and some cattle [W][31]. They grew barley and potatoes on the better-drained land in Village Bay [W][30]. One source adds oats [55]. Sources conflict on fishing. Wikipedia says the islanders generally eschewed fishing because of heavy seas and unpredictable weather [W]. Another source says the sea was too rough so they didn't eat fish [45]. An 1870s account says they fished for ling in summer [46]. Feathers were sold to the factor for six shillings per St Kilda stone of twenty-four pounds [68]. Fulmar oil was used as fuel [66][34]. Gannet skins were made into shoes [66]. In the 19th century, visiting steamers let islanders earn money selling tweeds and birds' eggs [W][33]. From the 1880s, trawlers brought additional trade [W]. The First World War introduced a money-based economy and regular contact with the outside world [W].

ECONOMIC ENGINE (TODAY): In 1955 the British government decided to incorporate St Kilda into a missile-tracking range based in Benbecula [W][39]. In 1957 St Kilda became permanently inhabited again [W]. The MOD leases St Kilda from the National Trust for Scotland for a nominal fee [W]. Civilians employed by defence contractor QinetiQ work at the base (MOD Hebrides) on a monthly rotation [W]. Conservation workers, volunteers and scientists spend time there in summer [W][40][42]. Long-term research studies the feral Soay sheep [W].

VIVID DETAILS AND ROUTINES: A 1764 census recorded the 90 inhabitants consuming '36 wildfoul eggs and 18 wildfoul' daily [W]. One report says each person ate 115 fulmars a year [52]. Each family had about three or four barrels of salted fulmars for winter [47]. Breakfast was thin porridge with a puffin boiled in it for flavour [48]. Dinner was roasted puffin with hard-boiled eggs [49]. One 1870s visitor calculated that eighty-nine thousand six hundred puffins had been killed [51]. Puffins were caught with fowling rods, flexible poles with a noose flicked over the bird's head [W]. Eggs were buried in peat ash to last the winter [W][32]. Fulmar oil was squeezed from the bird into the stomach of a solan goose used as a container [67]. Men climbed cliffs on ropes, sometimes barefoot, to take young birds and eggs [61][28]. Young women were sent to an island each year to catch puffins for feathers [62]. Fields were manured with puffin carcasses [56]. Grain was ground by handmills [57]. Every morning after prayers, all adult men met in the street as a 'parliament' to decide the day's work [W][58]. No one led the meeting [W]. Women also held meetings [60]. Bachelors proved themselves by balancing on one foot on the 'Mistress Stone', a door-shaped rock opening over a gully [W]. Food and gear were stored in cleitean, drystone huts with turf caps unique to St Kilda [W][53]. Wikipedia counts 1,260 cleitean on Hirta and 170 on the other islands [W]. Historic Environment Scotland counts over 1,400 across the archipelago [W]. Islanders signalled the mainland with a bonfire on Conachair [W][77]. They also launched the 'St Kilda mailboat', a wooden boat tied to a sheepskin bladder carrying a message, invented after John Sands' 1877 visit [W][74][76]. About two-thirds of these messages were found in western Scotland or Norway [W]. Sunday brought three compulsory services, each lasting two to three hours, under Rev. John Mackay [W].

SURPRISES: The north face of Conachair is the highest sea cliff in the UK [W][83]. Stac an Armin and Stac Lee are the highest sea stacks in Britain [W]. British soldiers searching for Bonnie Prince Charlie after 1746 found that the islanders had never heard of the prince or of King George II [W]. On 15 May 1918, the German submarine U-90 fired 72 shells at Hirta [W]. There was no loss of life, and 'one lamb was killed' [W]. No resident St Kildan is known to have fought in a war [W]. No serious crime by an islander was recorded in four centuries [W]. Neonatal tetanus caused infant mortality as high as 80 per cent in the late 19th century [W]. Of 56 live births in the 21 years before 1876, only 15 survived [W]. The daily 'parliament' influenced Enric Miralles' design for the Scottish Parliament Building [W]. The last great auk seen in Britain was killed on Stac an Armin in July 1840 [W]. The Soay sheep are believed to be remnants of the earliest sheep kept in Europe in the Neolithic Era [W]. The St Kilda wren and St Kilda field mouse are endemic subspecies [W][15].

DECLINE AND EVACUATION: After the First World War most young men left, and the population fell from 73 in 1920 to 37 in 1928 [W]. Crop failures followed [W]. Soil studies found lead contamination from manuring with seabird carcasses and peat ash [W]. Mary Gillies fell ill in January 1930 and was taken to the mainland, where she died [W]. Her death was assumed to be from appendicitis, but her son found in 1991 that it was pneumonia [W]. On 29 August 1930 HMS Harebell took the remaining 36 inhabitants to Morvern [W]. Wikipedia says this was a decision the islanders took collectively themselves [W]. The Gazetteer says the remaining population asked to leave [35]. Before leaving, the islanders left an open Bible and a pile of oats in each house and boarded at 7 am [W]. The working dogs were drowned in the bay because they could not be taken [W]. The last native St Kildan, Rachel Johnson, died in 2016 aged 93 [W]. In 1957 the National Trust for Scotland accepted the bequest of the islands, and in 1986 St Kilda became Scotland's first UNESCO World Heritage Site [W]. In 2005 it gained mixed status for both natural and cultural significance [W].

NOTES FOR EDITOR: Wikipedia is internally inconsistent on Lady Grange's confinement on Hirta, giving both 1734 to 1741 and 1734 to 1740 [W]. Sources differ on the date of the pier. Wikipedia says a jetty was completed in 1902 [W]. National Records of Scotland says a new pier was completed in 1901 [73].

POPULATION: Culion had 23,985 people in the 2024 census, a density of 48 inhabitants per square kilometre [W][25]. The 2020 census counted 23,213 people across 14 barangays [23][28]. One source gives a looser figure of around 20,000 people, including descendants of former leprosy patients [29]. Culion is a municipality in Palawan, Philippines, made up of Culion Island and 41 surrounding islands in the Calamian group [W]. The municipality covers 500 square kilometres of land, and Culion Island itself is 389 square kilometres [W]. It lies 287 kilometres north of Palawan's capital, Puerto Princesa City [53].

BEFORE THE COLONY: The original people of Culion are the Tagbanuas, who lived by fishing and food gathering [W]. Today they make up only about 8% of the population, and Barangay Carabao was created for them [W]. Early trading drew Calamianen and Cuyonon settlers from elsewhere in Palawan [W]. In the 1880s, French anthropologist Antoine-Alfred Marche described Culion as the principal village of the Calamianes, with a boat from Manila calling once a month [W]. On December 11, 1889, Justice of the Peace Claudio Sandoval y Rodríguez stamped a handwritten circular warning residents of penalties if caught gambling [W].

FOUNDING AS A LEPROSARIUM (WHO, WHEN, WHY): The American colonial government chose Culion as a segregation colony for people with leprosy [W][1]. This reflected a traditional belief that public health required isolating leprosy cases, a motive behind the creation of the Manila Board of Health [W]. One source says the initial impetus was protecting American soldiers [3]. At the time leprosy had no known cure, and Heiser estimated it affected more than six thousand people across the archipelago [2]. The island was chosen for its location at Palawan's northern tip and its isolation [8]. The reservation was modeled after Father Damien's leper colony on Molokai, Hawaii [22]. Culion was selected in 1901 [W]. On October 27, 1902, the Second Philippine Commission appropriated an initial $50,000, under Secretary of the Interior Dean C. Worcester and Director of Health Victor G. Heiser [W][10][11]. One source says Heiser was appointed Director of Health in 1905 [20]. On August 22, 1904, Civil Governor Luke E. Wright signed Executive Order No. 35, reserving Culion as a leper colony and government stock farm [W][12]. Private lands were purchased and residents obliged to leave [9]. Construction did not start until 1905 [14]. On May 27, 1906, the first contingent of patients arrived from Cebu aboard two Coast Guard cutters [W][14][15]. Wikipedia and one source put that contingent at 370 patients [W][14][15]. Other sources conflict: one says 670 patients from Cebu [78], and another says 150 patients from all over the Philippines [21]. Wikipedia names the cutters Polillo and Mindanao, while another source spells the first one Polilio [W][15]. The original 100-bed leprosarium had one physician, Dr. Charles F. de Mey, four French sisters of the Order of Saint Paul of Chartres, and a Jesuit [18]. Act 1711, passed September 12, 1907, made segregation of lepers compulsory under the Director of Health [W][16]. Between 1906 and 1910, the Americans rounded up 5,303 people with leprosy and brought them to the colony [W]. A numismatic source likewise describes about 5,300 patients on the island [79].

SIZE OF THE COLONY (CONFLICTING FIGURES): Some sources say the population peaked just short of 7,000 [30]. Another gives nearly 7,000 residents, including roughly 5,000 patients [31]. One source counts 6,500 people across 27 islands, with about 3,500 in the lepers' sector [40]. By contrast, other sources say patients numbered 16,138 by 1931 [32] or over 16,000 by 1931 [80]. One source even claims an all-time high of 31,803 by the end of 1980 [32]. That conflicts with reports that patients dwindled to 537 by 1980 [43] and to 739 residents by the late 1970s [44]. Several sources call Culion the largest leprosarium or leper colony in the world [31][80]. An estimated 50,000 people with leprosy were brought to the island over the decades [33].

LIFE AND ECONOMY INSIDE THE COLONY: Patients included ex-governors, lawyers, doctors, teachers and men of wealth, as well as laborers [74]. Most lived in small bamboo huts [69], and early conditions were described as chaotic [68]. Patients farmed and fished, selling their produce to the colony [70], and their stores were profitable [36]. The Culion Ice, Fish and Electric Company began in 1915 and was first financed entirely by inmates [35]. A steam-powered electrical plant provided 24-hour service and was operated by an American patient [72]. The colony had a patient police force [73]. It also had a civil court of fellow lepers and a market [37]. A Jesuit-initiated cooperative agricultural project aimed to develop 1,000 hectares [39].

THE LEPER MONEY: Culion had its own currency, used only on the island [W][38]. Officials feared, without scientific basis, that ordinary money could carry the disease [38]. The first coins, in aluminum, were issued in 1913 [W][59][64]. They came in ½-, 5-, 10- and 20-centavo and peso denominations [60]. Further issues were minted at the Manila Mint from 1920 to 1930 [W]. The 1925 Culion peso was copper-nickel and 35.4 mm across [76]. At first people refused the coins and threw them into the sea in contempt [64][65]. Anyone leaving had to convert leper money into government money [62]. Violators faced a fine, up to a month in prison, or both [63]. A special paper money issue was produced during World War II [W].

DECLINE AND TOWNHOOD: Culion began to decline with the financial crisis of 1933, when staff were cut [41]. After 1935 its population fell as new provincial leprosaria opened [42]. Patients were paroled by the thousands after new treatments based on the Mercado mixture, though many did not want to leave [75]. A 1964 Liberalization Act prohibited admission of new cases [45]. Leprosy on the island was abolished in the 1980s, but the WHO declared Culion leprosy-free only in 2006 [W][47]. President Corazon Aquino signed Republic Act 7193 creating the Municipality of Culion in 1992 [W][46]. Wikipedia gives two conflicting dates for this, February 19 and February 12, 1992 [W]. The first municipal elections were held on May 8, 1995, electing Mayor Hilarion Guia [W]. On October 29, 1998, the Department of Health handed control to the municipality, ending nearly a century of health-department rule [W]. The Culion Leprosy Archives were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register – Asia and the Pacific on June 18, 2018 [W].

ECONOMIC ENGINE TODAY: The economy rests mainly on fishery, agriculture and handicrafts, such as dried fish and bottled seafood production [54]. Dried fish-making and sawali-making are major manufacturing activities [55]. Culion's waters hold 201 fish species, including grouper, snapper and Spanish mackerel, along with squid, shrimp, crabs and sea cucumber [W]. Its reefs include 47 coral genera, 60% of the genera found in the Philippines [W]. Its coastline has 17 mangrove species and 9 seagrass species [W]. A survey found 52% of residents in Barangay Libis and 41% in Barangay Osmeña work in fisheries [48]. Even people in other jobs often fish as a sideline [49]. One resident told a reporter that in Culion everyone is a fisherman [50]. Culion hosts the only general hospital in the Calamian Islands [56]. Tourism is small but growing: Culion attracts visitors as an off-the-beaten-path alternative to Coron [58]. It placed eighth among 10 tracked areas in 2022 tourist data [57]. Its new tourism brand is 'Culion: The Paradise Regained' [W].

VIVID DETAILS FOR VISITORS: A giant eagle-above-a-shield symbol on a hillside greets arriving ferries, at the Aguila Viewpoint [89]. The old laboratory is now the Culion museum [90]. Sources conflict on the ferry. One reports one public ferry per day at Php 180 plus a Php 20 terminal fee [82][83]. Another reports two daily services at 325 PHP one way [84]. Visitors are advised to withdraw cash in Coron before boarding [86]. The 2019 film Culion depicts the island in the 1940s, when the disease was considered a life sentence [W].

raw_research: OVERVIEW: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are an Australian external territory in the Indian Ocean, roughly midway between Australia and Sri Lanka and relatively close to Sumatra [W]. The territory is two atolls of 27 coral islands, of which only West Island and Home Island are inhabited [W][56]. The atolls total 14.2 square kilometres, with a highest elevation of 5 metres, and are thickly covered with coconut palms [W]. There are no rivers or lakes, and fresh water comes only from underground rainwater lenses tapped by shallow bores or wells [W]. One travel guide calls the tap water drawn from this lens some of the freshest and purest drinking water in the world, and says old wells can still be seen on Home Island [81][82]. POPULATION: The 2021 Australian Census counted 593 people [W][51]. Another source gives 544 for 2016 [50]. Sources describe the total as around 600 [W][52][92]. Estimates for Home Island include more than 450 Cocos Malay people in the kampong [53], a population of 450 [91], and approximately 450 Cocos Malay across the islands [92]. As of 2001, approximately 80% of the population lived on Home Island [54]. The largest settlement is the village of Bantam on Home Island, while the capital is West Island [W]. In 2021, 65.6% identified as Muslim and 61.2% spoke Malay at home [W]. DISCOVERY AND NAME: Captain William Keeling of the East India Company sighted the islands in 1609 on a return voyage from the East Indies [W][1]. 'Cocos' refers to the abundant coconut trees [W]. The islands drew interest because they lay on a trade route from Europe to the Far East [2]. FOUNDING: Sources differ on dates. Scottish merchant seaman Captain John Clunies-Ross stopped at the islands in 1825 on a trip to India, nailed up a Union Jack and planned to return with his family [W]. One source specifies December 1825 and says he cleared land for cultivation [6]. Another source says the islands were not inhabited until 1826, when Englishman Alexander Hare established a settlement [3][24]. Another says Hare and Clunies-Ross had converged on the idea of settling the uninhabited islands by 1826 [11]. Hare, a wealthy Englishman and former resident of Banjarmasin in Borneo, reportedly felt 'he could not confine himself to the tame life that civilisation affords' [W]. One scholarly source says Dutch officials had blocked his plan to move to Java [9]. Hare was brought to the islands by Clunies-Ross's own brother, with what Wikipedia calls a volunteer harem of 40 Malay women [W]. A scholarly source instead describes Hare's people as captives, numbering about fifty-seven adult 'Natives of the Eastern Islands' and several dozen children [9][10]. Clunies-Ross returned in 1827 with his wife, children and mother-in-law, and found Hare already established [W][5]. Clunies-Ross was keen to exploit the islands' coconuts [5]. A feud followed, and Hare's women and followers gradually left him for Clunies-Ross's sailors and protection [W][17]. Hare left in 1831 [8]. Clunies-Ross and his family were left in sole possession in March 1831 [7]. Hare died in Bencoolen in 1834 [W]. Encouraged by members of the former harem, Clunies-Ross recruited Malays to come for work and wives [W]. Workers came from Java, Sumatra, Bali, Malacca, Bantam, Papua, the Malay peninsula and the Cape [18][19]. Wikipedia describes the islanders' ancestors as brought as indentured workers, slaves or convicts [W]. DARWIN: HMS Beagle, under Captain Robert FitzRoy, arrived on 1 April 1836 [W][20]. Charles Darwin's observations there supported his theory of atoll formation, later published as The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs [W]. Darwin's assistant Syms Covington noted the Ross family living with 'about sixty or seventy mulattos from the Cape of Good Hope' [W][20]. THE COPRA FIEFDOM (THE ORIGINAL ECONOMIC ENGINE): The Clunies-Ross family ruled the islands as a private fiefdom [W]. Wikipedia says this lasted almost 150 years, while another source says 150 years [W][8]. For many years the islands were a powerhouse of copra production, with all resources and workers devoted to coconut growing and processing [14][25]. Home Island held the family, the Cocos Malay workforce, and the buildings and machines for production [26]. Workers were paid in Cocos rupees, a currency Clunies-Ross minted himself and which could only be redeemed at the company store [W][27]. Workers could not own land, could not leave without permission, and had no legal recourse against the estate [28]. One islander remembers his parents working from dawn until dusk to pick enough coconuts to pay for their rations [29]. This way of life continued until the 1970s [30]. Britain annexed the islands in 1857 through Captain Stephen Grenville Fremantle of HMS Juno [W][21]. The shire's history says Fremantle made a mistake, because he was supposed to annex a different set of Cocos Islands [22]. In 1886, Queen Victoria granted the islands in perpetuity [W][23]. Wikipedia names the recipient as John Clunies-Ross [W]. Another source says the grant went to his grandson George and his heirs [23]. END OF THE ERA: Sources differ on when the coconut industry ended. One says the coconut fibre industry ceased in 1980 [38]. Another says the Home Island copra industry folded in the 1980s [37]. A third says the industry ceased only in 1987 [15]. A 1974 UN mission criticised the Australian government over conditions [31][35]. In 1978, Australia forced the family to sell for A$6,250,000, using the threat of compulsory acquisition [W][4][34]. The family kept its home, Oceania House, by agreement [W][34]. In 1983 the government reneged and told John Clunies-Ross to leave [W]. The High Court ruled the resumption of Oceania House unlawful [W]. However, a government ban on business with his shipping company contributed to his bankruptcy, and he moved to Perth [W]. Some family members still live on Cocos [W]. On 6 April 1984, all 261 eligible islanders voted in a UN-supervised referendum [W]. The result was 229 for integration with Australia, 21 for free association, nine for independence, and two who gave no preference [W]. WHAT KEEPS PEOPLE THERE NOW: Economic activity is limited, and the public sector provides most employment [40]. One source puts the public sector at 50% of employment, centred on West Island [42]. The same source says inhabitants are largely supported financially by the Commonwealth government [43]. The Cocos Islands Cooperative Society employs construction workers, stevedores and lighterage workers [W]. The cooperative also runs the inter-island ferry and buses and owns the West Island supermarket and the Home Island hardware store [W][80]. Wikipedia describes a small and growing tourist industry based on water and nature activities [W]. One overview says tourism draws approximately 250 visitors a year and is hampered by isolation [44]. Small businesses offer accommodation, tourism, mechanical services, gardening and cleaning [41]. West Island residents are primarily mainland Australians working on government contracts for 2–3 years [46][54]. Unemployment was 6.7% in 2011 [W]. The same overview recorded 7.9% in 1996, 12.1% in 2001 and 4.7% in 2006 [48]. That overview also says the unofficial unemployment rate is considerably higher than the official rate [49]. STRATEGIC ROLE: In 1901 a telegraph cable station on Direction Island became a hub of the All Red Line [W]. That station was attacked in both world wars [W]. On 9 November 1914, HMAS Sydney defeated the German cruiser SMS Emden, which beached itself on North Keeling Island [W]. Emden lost 134 killed, compared with four killed aboard Sydney [W]. Fifty Germans from the shore party commandeered a schooner and escaped, eventually reaching Constantinople [W]. In 1942, a mutiny in the Ceylon Defence Force garrison led to three executions [W]. These were the only British Commonwealth soldiers executed for mutiny in the Second World War [W]. The airstrip is more than 2 km long [W]. It is being extended by 150 metres for P-8 Poseidon surveillance aircraft, with completion scheduled by 2026 [W]. The United States has used it as a stopover between Diego Garcia and Guam [W]. A joint Indo-Australian team has set up antennae to track India's Gaganyaan crewed spacecraft [W]. ISOLATION AND DAILY LIFE: Perth is about 3,000 km away, and serious medical cases are sent there [W][60]. Sources differ on flights. Wikipedia says QantasLink flies from Perth twice a week [W]. A travel source says there is a weekly Virgin Australia service [68]. Most food must be imported [W][45]. In 2015, residents paid $12 for one cucumber and up to $19 for a rockmelon [62]. Perishables and mail were sometimes left on the tarmac in Perth [61]. Air freighters from Perth run fortnightly [57]. Non-priority mail goes by sea and can take up to two months [W]. The ferry costs AUD$2.50 each way and the bus AUD$0.50 [73][74][76]. The ferry runs daily except Sunday [72][88]. Wednesday is popular for weekly Cocos Malay buffet dinners on Home Island [88]. The call to prayer is broadcast five times a day on Home Island [83]. Home Island has a mosque, two cafes, one supermarket and a post office [84]. Cocos Malays keep weekend shacks called pondoks on most of the larger islands [W][90]. Historically, expeditions went to North Keeling to collect coconuts, ironwood timber and red-footed boobies [32]. Once a month, the Jukong and Sailing Club races jukongs in the lagoon off Home Island, and locals watch from buggies [89][79]. Young Cocos Malays travel to Perth to finish high school [87]. SURPRISES: The Cocos Islands Golf Club, established in 1962, is the only golf course in the world played across an international airport runway [W]. In 2016, a Direction Island beach was named Australia's best beach [W]. A 2019 study estimated 414 million pieces of plastic weighing 238 tonnes on the islands, 93% of it buried under sand [W]. The territory's internet domain is .cc [W]. North Keeling's Pulu Keeling National Park, established on 12 December 1995, holds the only surviving population of the endangered Cocos Buff-banded Rail [W]. As of 2019, Cocos Malay descendants were seeking recognition as Indigenous Australians [W].

raw_research:
FOUNDING AND ORIGINS: Vardø is a town on the island of Vardøya in the Barents Sea, just off the coast of the Varanger Peninsula, and is the administrative centre of Vardø Municipality in Finnmark county, Norway [W]. Archaeological excavations show evidence of settlements in the area around Vardø that are more than 4,500 years old [18]. The village became important because of Vardøhus Fortress, built on the island in the early 14th century [W][17][8]. Sources differ on the exact date: one says the first fortress was erected around 1300 [1], another says it dates to 1306 [3], and the Archbishop of Nidaros (Trondheim) consecrated the first church in Vardø in 1307, by which date the fortress is inferred to have been built [11]. Vardø is first mentioned in history in 1307, when a church and fortress were built there [12]. The builder was King Håkon V Magnusson [1][3]. His aims were to assert Norwegian sovereignty in the north and secure tax revenues from Finnmark [1][2]. Other sources say it was built to oversee the fur and fish trade and to watch the Russians [7], or as protection against the powerful Russian Novgorod Republic [8]. In 1251 an embassy from the Republic of Novgorod complained to King Haakon IV Haakonson of Norway about clashes between Norwegians and Karelians [9]. One source states there never was an actual war, but there were conflicts about the tribute of Sami tribes [4]. A permanent settlement gradually formed around the citadel, with residents living under the protection of the garrison [16][W]. The current Vardøhus Fortress is the third on the site [13]. A second fortification was built around 1450, and neither early structure has visible remains above ground today [14]. The present fortress was built between 1734 and 1738 [15]. The name comes from the island, Vardøya; the Old Norse form Vargøy used vargr, meaning wolf, which around 1500 was replaced with varða, meaning cairn, while øy means island [W].

TOWN STATUS AND POMOR TRADE: Vardø grew into a major trading post between Norwegians in Finnmark and nearby Russians [W]. Pomor trade was very important in the 18th century, and Vardø was often called the Pomor capital [W][23]. Because of this trade, Vardø was granted town status as a kjøpstad in 1789 [W][23]. Its town charter is dated 17 July 1789, making it one of the oldest towns in Northern Norway [19]. The charter was issued by Christian VII of Denmark-Norway, who gave charters to Vardø and Hammerfest in 1789 [20]. Wikipedia describes the grantor only as the King of Norway [W]. One source says Vardø was officially founded in 1789 but has a much longer history [25]. Market town status legalised and strengthened barter with White Sea merchants [21]. One source dates the Pomor trade from about 1740 until the Russian revolution in 1917 [22], while another places the Pomor period from the 18th to the 20th century [32]. Russian grain products were bartered for Norwegian fish [31]. The Pomors brought flour and wood, and because the Russian Orthodox fast banned them from eating meat, fish became an important trade commodity [33]. Barter later became money trade [34]. The Russian ruble was hard currency, and Vardø had its own Russian bakeries [35]. A unique language, Russian-Norwegian, was spoken among fish mongers [35]. Until 1850 Vardø was a small fishing community, but between 1850 and 1910 its population increased dramatically [24][36]. It was once Norway's largest fishing village, with some 4,000 inhabitants [37].

DARK CHAPTERS: In the 17th century Vardø was the centre of several high-profile witch trials, most notably in 1621 and 1662 [W]. In 1944 the city's historic buildings were almost completely destroyed by massive Allied bombing and by arson [41]. The population has declined since World War II [40].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: Fishing has been the basis of survival and the main economic activity [29]. The largest industry in the town is fishing and fish processing [W][38]. Residents mainly rely on fishing-related industries for their living [90]. Several fish companies produce fresh and frozen fish for national and international markets [44]. Vardø had more fishermen in 2019 than in 1983 [45]. Coastal fishers also create jobs on land, including processing and packaging fish, preparing lines, and repair and maintenance [47]. The town has a good port, with another at Svartnes on the mainland [W]. Sources differ on the biggest employer: one names the public sector [42], while another says the armed forces are the biggest employer apart from the local authorities [48]. A growing private sector includes trade, service, fish industry, tourism and technology [43]. A new shipping traffic control centre has been built, and tourism is increasingly important [51]. The municipality's debt exceeds 30 million euros, or 15,000 euros per inhabitant, according to Statistics Norway figures [52]. The decline of the fishing industry has led to population loss [38]. Most young people move to other Norwegian cities, leaving mainly pensioners [39].

GLOBUS RADAR: Wikipedia says the town has housed the GLOBUS I, II and III radar installations since 1998 [W]. Another source says the GLOBUS radar system has stood on the hill above Vardø since the 1950s, always as a cooperation between Norway and the USA [50]. The official purpose is tracking space junk [W]. Because of the site's proximity to Russia and an alleged link to US anti-missile systems, it has caused heated controversy in diplomatic and intelligence circles [W]. GLOBUS III began construction in 2016 and became operational in 2023 [W]. The Russian military considers the station a threat to its national security [W]. Few people know how many employees work at the radar [49]. Criticising the radar may be a hard opinion to voice locally [28].

WHAT IS SURPRISING: Vardø is the easternmost town in Norway and in all the Nordic countries [W][27]. At 31°E, it lies east of Saint Petersburg, Kyiv and Istanbul [W]. Eastern Finnmark shares the national time zone, but it is more than an hour at odds with daylight hours [W][86]. Vardø sits at 70.2 degrees north [27]. It is described as Norway's only town with an arctic climate, a classification at risk from global warming [67]. Another source says it used to have a tundra climate but is now considered subarctic due to climate change [68]. Local lore holds that Vardø has only one tree, an old rowan [63]. The rowan at the fortress is wrapped and protected every winter [64]. From above, Vardø resembles a butterfly, with its parts joined by a low neck of land [85].

CONCRETE DETAILS: The town covers 1.2 square kilometres, giving a density of 1,439 inhabitants per square kilometre [W]. The surrounding sea remains ice-free even in winter [54]. February is the coldest month, averaging -4.1 °C [55]. August is the warmest month, averaging about 10 °C [58]. The record low is -22.7 °C, set in February 1929 [56]. Winters are long, freezing, snowy, extremely windy and overcast [57]. The sun stays below the horizon for about 1.9 months in winter [59]. At the end of January, after two months of darkness, the fortress fires a salute to celebrate the sun's return, and the day is marked with school holidays [60]. In summer the day lasts on average 24 hours [61]. One visitor wears wool even in summer [62].

TRANSPORT: The undersea Vardø Tunnel, part of European route E75, connects the town to the mainland [W]. The airport at Svartnes lies at the tunnel's other end [W]. That airport is 4.5 km outside the city [77]. Tunnel length is given as 2.8 km [69], 2.7 km [75] and 2,892 metres [76]. It reaches 88 metres below sea level [70][74][76]. One source says it opened in 1982 as Norway's first subsea road tunnel [73]. Another says it opened in 1983 [74]. It was officially opened by King Olav V [72]. Vardø is a stop on the Norwegian Coastal Express [78]. The northbound ferry docks around 3am and the southbound around 4pm [79]. In winter, visitors are advised to wear boots with spikes because the streets can be icy [84]. During winter, skrei (migratory Arctic cod) is the culinary highlight, and locals eat a traditional dish called mølje [87]. Coffee is consumed in large quantities to combat the cold [89].

POPULATION: Wikipedia gives the town's 2023 population as 1,727 [W]. Another source says the municipality had 1,900 inhabitants in the third quarter of 2022, of whom 1,700 lived in the administrative centre [26]. Other figures include 1,897 [27], about 1,700 [91], fewer than 2,000 [90], and just over 2,000 [28][37].
