raw_research:
FOUNDING: After Napoleon's defeat, the Congress of Vienna of 1814–15 redrew Europe's borders, and the district of Moresnet became a sticking point between the new United Kingdom of the Netherlands and the Kingdom of Prussia [W][3][4]. Both wanted the valuable zinc mine there, called Altenberg in German and Vieille Montagne in French [W][4]. Zinc was needed to make zinc and brass [W][5]. At the time, Bristol was the only other place where zinc ore was processed, according to one account [W]. Another source calls Bristol one of the few other places in Europe processing zinc [6]. The mine's concession had been granted in 1805 to the Liège chemist Jean-Jacques Daniel Dony [17]. One scholarly source says the territory's history resulted from a misunderstanding [13]. It notes that Article 25 of the Vienna Final Act annexed Moresnet to Prussia, while Article 66 placed the province under Dutch sovereignty [14]. Another source says the Congress of Vienna assigned the Moresnet area to the Netherlands in 1815 [15]. Dutch and Prussian representatives met in nearby Aachen in December 1815 [W][1]. They reached a compromise on 26 June 1816 [W][2]. The deal split the district three ways [W][7]. The village of Moresnet went to the Dutch Liège Province [W][7]. Prussian Moresnet, later renamed Neu-Moresnet, went to the Prussian Rhine Province [W][7]. The mine and the adjacent village became a neutral territory pending a future agreement [W]. Neither power's army was allowed to occupy it, and the two ran it jointly as a condominium [W][8]. One source describes this provisional arrangement as lasting 104 years [9]. Border markers were formally installed on 23 September 1818 [W][12]. When Belgium became independent in 1830, it took over the Dutch role [W][11]. Wikipedia adds that the Dutch never formally ceded their claim [W]. The territory existed from 1816 to 1920 [W][40].

SHAPE AND SIZE: It was 1.5 km wide and 2.5 km long, covering about 3.5 square kilometres [W][40]. It was roughly triangular [W][10]. Its base was the Aachen–Liège road, and two straight lines converged on the Vaalserberg [W]. After 1830, its northern tip formed a quadripoint with Dutch Limburg, the Prussian Rhine Province and Belgian Liège Province [W]. That point is now represented by the Three-Country Point of Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands [W]. At its creation, the territory held only about fifty houses with 256 people, plus a church and the mine [10]. The 256 figure is dated to 1815 by some sources [W][35] and to 1816 by others [32][68].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: Life was dominated by the Vieille Montagne mining company, the principal employer [W][19][70]. The company also operated residences, shops, a hospital and a bank [W][19][49]. One historian called it 'a company town in the truest sense', with the company supplying jobs, housing, healthcare and commerce [20]. The company built a school, two churches, houses and a pharmacy, and paid for teachers, priests and a doctor [51]. In 1857 it funded a school and lent one of its supervisors to the mayor to serve as village policeman [22][50]. Some company directors were appointed mayors, and the communal centre was housed in company premises [21]. Women washed lead, zinc and iron at the site [52]. Heavily loaded wagons laboured up the valley slopes, and the air reeked of sulphur and lead [54].

Population growth was driven by workers drawn from neighbouring countries [W][35][70]. Sources agree on about 500 inhabitants in 1830 [33][34]. For 1858 they conflict: 2,275 by one count [W][35] versus 2,572 by another [33][34][36][68]. One breakdown of the 2,572 lists 700 true 'Neutrals' (descendants of the original population), 850 Belgians, 800 Prussians and 200 Dutch [36]. Another gives 695 born in the neutral zone and 852 Belgians [68]. Wikipedia gives 4,668 for 1914 [W][35]. Other final figures vary: about 4,500 by the time the territory disappeared [37], up to 3,500 [39], and 3,000 [40]. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gave the village 2,800 inhabitants [38].

Sources conflict on when the mine closed: most say 1885 [W][28][31], but one says zinc extraction ended in 1895 [29]. The company later resumed operation as a zinc smelting factory and remained the principal employer [30]. One source says the closure was not especially worrying economically because numerous businesses were flourishing by then [31]. Zinc was the territory's most important income, but cheap goods, liquor and gambling also mattered [26].

OTHER DRAWS: Taxes were low, and the budget was fixed at 2,735 Belgian francs for most of the territory's history [W][23][56][57]. Neither neighbour levied import tariffs, and one source adds there were no customs checkpoints [W][23][56][57]. Prices were lower than just across the border [W][57]. Food, clothing, coffee and alcohol were cheap, along with coveted smuggled goods [55]. The territory became a haven for smugglers [23]. One source says criminals fled there because there were no extradition treaties [77]. Residents were authorised to distil alcohol tax-free for personal use [27]. Around the early 1900s there were three gin distilleries [W][60]. Many immigrants came to escape military service [W][76]. Neutrals were considered stateless and thus exempt from conscription [W][24]. Belgium began conscripting its relocated citizens in 1854, and Prussia followed in 1874 [W][65]. After that, the exemption covered only descendants of the original inhabitants [W]. A conflicting source says residents had no military service only until 1847 [25].

GOVERNANCE: Most sources say two royal commissioners, one from each neighbour, governed the territory [W][9][61]. Wikipedia places them in Belgian Verviers and Prussian Eupen [W]. Another source puts the Prussian commissioner in Aachen and the Belgian in Verviers [63]. The commissioners appointed a mayor [W][63]. The Napoleonic codes remained in force [W][61]. There was no court in the territory, so outside judges came in to decide cases [W][62]. Wikipedia says these judges were Belgian and Prussian [W], while another source says Prussian and Dutch [62]. There was no appeal [W]. From 1859, a ten-member advisory council appointed by the mayor existed [W][64]. Residents had no vote [W][24][64], and one source adds they could not join a trade union [64]. Mail and most services were shared between Belgium and Prussia [W][66]. There were five schools [W].

The territory had no currency of its own [W]. The French franc was legal tender, and Prussian/German, Belgian and Dutch money also circulated [W][58]. Local coins from 1848 were unofficial [W][59]. From 1883 a black-white-blue horizontal tricolour served as the flag, though its origin is unknown [W].

SURPRISES: In 1886, the mine's chief doctor Wilhelm Molly tried to launch a local postal service with its own stamps, but Belgium quickly thwarted it [W]. One source names his association the 'Kelmis Verkehrs-Anstalt zu Neutral Moresnet' [67]. A casino opened in August 1903 after Belgium closed its own casinos [W][71][73]. Locals were barred from gambling there, and no more than 20 people could gather at a time [W][72]. It was abandoned when Kaiser Wilhelm II threatened to partition the territory or cede it to Belgium [W][73]. In 1908 Molly proposed making Neutral Moresnet the first Esperanto state, named Amikejo ('friendship-place') [W]. Its proposed anthem was set to the tune of 'O Tannenbaum' [W]. A rally was held in Kelmis on 13 August 1908 [W]. The World Congress of Esperanto in Dresden declared the territory the world capital of Esperanto [W]. Karl Schriewer, a 19-year-old Esperantist from Kelmis, promised to teach Esperanto four times a week [74]. Around 1900, Germany was accused of sabotage and obstruction to force the issue [W]. Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August 1914 [W]. A total of 147 citizens were killed [W]. Prussia annexed the territory on 27 June 1915, but the annexation was never internationally recognised [W]. The Treaty of Versailles, signed 28 June 1919, awarded it to Belgium, effective 10 January 1920 [W]. It was renamed Kelmis (La Calamine), after kelme, the dialect word for zinc spar [W]. Mayor Pierre Grignard stayed on as Kelmis's first mayor [W].

TODAY: Germany re-annexed the area in World War II, and it was returned to Belgium in 1944 [W]. Kelmis has been part of Belgium's German-speaking community since 1973 [W]. In 1977 it absorbed Neu-Moresnet and Hergenrath [W][43]. Kelmis had 11,000 people in 2018 [41]. Another source gives 10,881 as of 2011, over 18.1 square kilometres [42]. Of the 60 border markers, more than 50 still stand [W]. The Museum Vieille Montagne occupies the former administration buildings on Lütticher Strasse [W][45]. Rare yellow calamine pansies (Viola lutea calaminaria) now flourish on the old waste heaps [53]. Carnival societies survive, and the annual Kirmes fair began in Neutral Moresnet [75]. The company survives as VMZINC, part of Umicore [W][46].

raw_research:
WHERE AND WHAT: Aogashima is a volcanic island and the southernmost, most isolated inhabited island of the Izu Islands, lying about 358 km south of mainland Tokyo and 64 km south of Hachijō-jima [W]. It is administered as the village of Aogashima under Hachijō Subprefecture, governed by Tokyo, and has the smallest population of any municipality in Japan [W][19]. Sources disagree on its area: 8.75 km2 [W] versus 5.96 km2 [16]. The island is 3.5 km long and at most 2.5 km wide, formed by overlapping remnants of at least four submarine calderas and ringed by very steep cliffs [W]. The Ikenosawa caldera, 1.5 km across, dominates the island and holds a secondary cone named Maruyama; the highest point, Otonbu on the caldera's southern ridge, is 423 m [W]. The Japan Meteorological Agency still rates it a Class-C active volcano [W].

POPULATION: Wikipedia gives 170 people as of 2014 [W]. A Tokyo government page gives 162 as of R6.9.1 (1 September 2024) [16]. Another source cites official 2025 statistics of 156 registered residents [17]. Wikivoyage gives 205 as of 2009 [18]. One source says the population slipped from around 170 a decade ago to about 160 now, and is aging [20]. The historical peak is given as 754 in 1881 [13], as around 750 by the early 1900s [21], and as over 700 in the late 1800s [22].

EARLY HISTORY: The history of human settlement on Aogashima is uncertain [W][4]. No prehistoric artifacts whatsoever have been discovered on the island [1]. A record titled the Hachijojima-Kojima, Aogashima Nendaiki (1474) gives an account of a ship that lost its way returning from Hachijojima [3]. Edo-period records kept at Hachijō-jima note volcanic activity in 1652 and from 1670 to 1680 [W]. One source says people lived on Aogashima fishing and farming before 1785 [35]. One source says the volcanic soil could support hardy crops such as sweet potatoes and the surrounding waters were full of fish [36]. The same source says remote, dangerous islands like this offered free land, fertile soil and total autonomy [37].

THE DISASTER: An earthquake swarm in July 1780 was followed by steam rising from lakes in the Ikenosawa caldera, and further earthquakes in May 1781 led to an eruption [W]. In April 1783, lava flows from the Maruyama cone forced the evacuation of all 63 households on the island [W][5]. In 1785 a massive eruption struck a population of 327 [W][6]. Estimates of the dead are 130–140 [W][7], roughly two in five [7], or around 130 [38]. One source's headline instead says the eruption killed half its people [14]. One account records around 200 survivors escaping on rescue boats sent from Hachijojima [8]. One source says people drowned, others died of illness, and by 1802 the island was deserted again [9]. There has been no significant volcanic activity since the 18th century [W].

RESETTLEMENT (the founding of today's community): In 1817, 15 years after the island had emptied, a petition to rebuild was made [10]. An advance party of 20 landed, led by Sasaki Jirodayu, whom one writer calls "the Moses of Aogashima" [11]. Sources differ on the date of the return. One encyclopedia cited dates it to 1834, when the islanders formed the villages that stand today [12]. Another source says a resettlement led by an official named Sasaki brought people back in 1835 [15]. A shogunate land survey took place in 1835 [12]. The island sat empty for roughly half a century, or about 50 years [15][38]. About 240 people lived there at the time of the return [13]. Another source cites a census of 241 returners, most of them fishers [14].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: Sources describe the economy differently. One describes it as a modest mix of subsidies, tourism, salt production and shochu distilling [24]. Another says the pillars are fishing, agriculture and, more importantly, salt production [28]. Others cite farming and fishing plus public service and limited tourism [29], or fishing, a little farming and limited tourism [30]. Another names fishing and camellia farming [31]. Two sources stress dependence on the state. One says residents rely heavily on government assistance [25]. Another says roughly 70 of the island's 170 residents are government workers transferred in for short-term posts [23]. One source counters that fishing is difficult and agriculture very limited [51]. Another says that without reliable shipping or modern infrastructure, building sustainable industry remains difficult [34]. The village lists its specialty goods as shochu, Japanese black beef and salt, among others [16]. The island has a shochu distillery [54]. In 2024, "Tokyo Island Sake," a shochu brand from the Izu Islands that includes Aogashima shochu, was designated a Geographical Indication [26]. Accommodation is often booked out by construction workers [65].

SURPRISING / VIVID DETAILS: One source says about 160 people live inside the crater of an active volcano [14]. Another says the small town center sits exclusively on the outside of the volcano [32]. Locals call the natural steam vents hingya [59]. The vents power the village's public sauna and a communal steam cooker [59]. The geothermal steam cooker is free to use [61]. Visitors can cook eggs and sweet potatoes in it [60]. The Aogashima Fureai Sauna has showers and a communal bath [60][62]. Hingya steam is also used to evaporate deep-sea water into a signature salt product whose name begins "Kuroshio Hingya" [63]. With very little light pollution, the island is a stargazing site where the Milky Way can be seen on a good night [58]. Aogashima is an Important Bird Area supporting Japanese woodpigeons, Pleske's grasshopper warblers, Ijima's leaf-warblers and Izu thrushes [W]. It is also part of Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park [W].

DAILY LIFE: Sources disagree on amenities. One lists 1 grocery store, 1 post office, 3 bars and no hospital, with helicopter evacuation needed for emergencies [52]. Another says the island has a small general store and a single bar [53]. There are no convenience stores or ATMs, and mobile signal is limited [55]. Sources agree there is one school [53][56]. One describes it as an elementary and junior high school [53]. Another says it houses elementary, junior high and high school under one roof, with a few students per class [56]. Most residents travel by car rather than walking or biking [57]. Lodging is a few small B&Bs plus a free campsite [33][66]. There are no beaches [68].

GETTING THERE: Travelers first reach Hachijojima from Tokyo, then take a helicopter or ferry [39]. The helicopter takes about 20 minutes and has 9 seats [40]. Helicopter service began in 1993; before that, passengers, goods and food arrived by boat only [49]. Fog from the steamy crater can ground the helicopter [46]. The ferry takes about 2.5–3 hours [40][41] and costs 2,520 yen one-way [41]. About 40% of boat service is canceled due to rough waves, and sometimes no boat runs for over a week [44][45]. Each day a speaker broadcast tells the village whether the boat is running [47]. When the announcement is a cancellation, residents calmly say "Not again" [48]. The small port is mostly used by fishermen [50]. Bookings open only one month ahead, by phone at exactly 9am [42].

FOUNDING: Longyearbyen is named after the American John Munro Longyear and was established by him through the Arctic Coal Company, which started coal mining there in 1906 [W][6]. One source instead says the town was founded in 1905 as a coal-mining settlement by an American company and named after J. M. Longyear [15]. Longyear first visited Svalbard as a tourist or cruise passenger in 1901 [W][2][27]. One source describes him then as a 51-year-old businessman from Michigan with interests in mines, railways and banking [5]. On that visit he saw commercial potential in the rich coal deposits [7]. He returned in 1903 and met Henrik B. Næss in Adventfjorden, who gave him coal samples and information on coal fields [W][3]. With his associate Frederick Ayer, Longyear bought the Norwegian claims on the west side of Adventfjorden and expanded them significantly the following year [W][4]. In 1906 the Boston-based Arctic Coal Company, with Ayer and Longyear as main shareholders, began mining in Mine 1a after building docks and housing [W][6]. The company had American administration but mostly Norwegian labourers and called the town Longyear City [W]. The site on Adventfjorden gave convenient access both to coal seams and to the sea for shipping [8]. A tourism-board source states plainly that Longyearbyen exists because of the coal in the mountains and was built by the mining industry over the past century [9]. Coal had been harvested commercially on Svalbard before this, by Søren Zakariassen in 1899 [W]. Tourism also predates the town: tours to Hotellneset began in 1896 with a prefabricated hotel, which closed after the 1897 season [W]. After financial difficulties during the First World War, Store Norske Spitsbergen Kulkompani (SNSK), incorporated on 30 November 1916, bought the mining operations [W][12][28]. The town was renamed Longyearbyen in 1926 [W][13]. One source links the renaming to Store Norske's ownership [13]. Another source dates the renaming to around SNSK's 1916 takeover, saying it came a decade after founding [28]. The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 gave Norway sovereignty and came into effect in 1925 [W]. Another source gives the signing date as 9 February 1920 and entry into force as 14 August 1925 [14]. The treaty gives 45 countries equal rights for mineral exploitation [43].

WAR AND REBUILDING: In 1941 Operation Gauntlet evacuated the population, and on 3 September 1941 765 people were evacuated from Longyearbyen to Scotland [W]. The German Kriegsmarine almost completely destroyed the town on 8 September 1943 [W][17][18]. One source gives the date instead as 8 August 1943 [16]. The attack used the battleships Tirpitz and Scharnhorst plus nine destroyers [W]. Only four buildings survived: the hospital, the power station, an office building and a residential building [W]. By 1948 coal production had returned to the pre-war level of 480,000 tonnes per year [W].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: For most of its history Longyearbyen was a company town [W]. Store Norske controlled not only the mines but also housing and other aspects of life [30]. SNSK even issued its own banknotes at par with the Norwegian krone, which were withdrawn from 1980 [W]. Private car ownership was permitted by SNSK only from 1982 [W]. The opening of the airport in 1975, giving a year-round connection to the mainland, dramatically transformed society [W][31]. In the 1990s the authorities began 'normalising' the town by ending the company-town scheme and introducing local democracy and a varied economy [W]. Most mining moved to Sveagruva in the 1990s, and production there ceased in 2017 after large financial losses since 2014 [W]. Coal production peaked in 2007 at 4.1 million tonnes [W]. Mining was not profitable and relied on state subsidies [W]. Mine 7, the last Norwegian coal mine on Svalbard, closed on 30 June 2025 [W]. Another source likewise says Norwegian coal mining on Svalbard has concluded [39]. The Wikipedia lead, however, still states that SNSK 'still conducts mining' [W]. The coal-fired power plant was shut down on 19 October 2023, and the town switched to imported diesel for electricity and heat [41]. Many residents criticise the economic and environmental costs of that diesel dependence [42]. Tourism, research and education are now the town's mainstays [W][39]. Tourism and related services are described as the primary economic sector [35]. Tourism mainly employs non-Norwegian residents [38]. Guest-nights rose from 30,000 in 1995 to 89,000 in 2008 [W]. Tourism revenue in 2007 was NOK 291 million [W]. Around 72,500 guests arrived in 2018 and around 70,000 in 2023 [37]. According to Visit Svalbard, 67,656 tourists visited in 2024 [36]. The University Centre in Svalbard opened on 6 September 1993 with 30 students [W]. It now has 350 students and offers semester courses rather than degrees [W]. All its students must complete mandatory training in firearms and snowmobiling [78]. Svalbard Satellite Station exists because of the town's excellent location for downloading data from polar-orbiting satellites [W]. Fisheries are growing as cod, mackerel and snow crab move north with warming waters [W]. Norway values the Svalbard fishing trade at about US$94 million a year [W]. Public funding to Svalbard society rose from NOK 380 million in 2008 to NOK 650 million in 2015 [W]. Income tax is lower than on the mainland and there is no VAT, because the treaty limits taxation [W]. The local council says the town should not be a lifelong community [26].

SURPRISES: Burials have not been allowed since 1950 [W]. The ban followed the discovery that bodies of 1918 flu victims had not decomposed in the permafrost [W]. Terminally ill residents are typically required to move to the mainland [W]. Pregnant women leave weeks before delivery because the local hospital cannot handle complex births [75]. Importing most live mammals and birds is prohibited [W][72]. That ban is intended to protect the fragile flora and fauna [71]. Monthly alcohol purchases are restricted [W]. Anyone leaving the settlement must carry suitable means of scaring off polar bears [44]. Wikipedia describes carrying a rifle outside the settlement as a recommendation [W]. Signs ask people not to bring firearms into shops [45]. Buildings have special safes for weapons [46]. Foreigners need no visa or work permit to live there [W]. However, people without income can be rejected by the governor [W]. No care, nursing services or welfare payments are available [W]. Longyearbyen was called the fastest-warming town in the world as of 2021 [W]. Mean annual temperature rose by 3.6 °C between the 1961–1990 and 1991–2020 averages [W]. The record high of 21.7 °C was set in July 2020 [W]. The town has the lowest recorded average UV index of any inhabited place, at 0.75 [W]. Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in 2008 [W]. Its site was chosen for its remoteness, sound geology and permafrost temperature [W]. In an abandoned coal mine, the Arctic World Archive has stored data since 27 March 2017, including all of GitHub's open-source code [W].

VIVID DETAILS: Midnight sun lasts from 18 April to 24 August [W]. Another source gives the dates as 20 April to 22 August [49]. Polar night lasts from 27 October to 15 February [W][48]. Because of mountain shading, sunlight does not reach most of the town until around 8 March [W]. That date is celebrated with Solfestuka, the Sun Festival Week [W]. Thick blackout curtains help residents sleep through the midnight sun [50]. In 2008 there were 2,672 snowmobiles, more than residents [W]. That number had risen to 2,873 by 2022 [55]. By comparison, in 1969 there were 140 snowmobiles and just 33 cars [W]. Locals park their snowmobiles on wooden pallets in summer to protect the tundra [57]. The 50 km road network connects to no other community [W]. Svalbardbutikken is the only grocery store [W][59]. It has about 50 employees from 13 nationalities [60]. Sold-out products can take up to 10 days to be restocked by ship [61]. Buildings stand on wooden or steel piles to protect the permafrost [73]. Residents remove their shoes in many homes, hotels and even offices [74]. Thais have been the largest minority, numbering 137 people in 2020 [W]. Thai residents first arrived in the 1970s, when men brought wives from Thailand [W]. In 2022, 43% of residents had stayed less than two years [W]. The government calls this a 'revolving door society' [W]. In 70% of households a single person lives alone [W].

POPULATION: Wikipedia estimates the population at around 2,400–2,800 [W]. The tax office registered 2,354 residents on 31 August 2020 [W]. One source says roughly 2,400 [21]. Another says about 2,500, more than half of them non-Norwegian [22]. That conflicts with Wikipedia, which puts Norwegians at 64.5% in 2020 [W]. A further source counts 2,556 people in Longyearbyen and Ny-Ålesund combined on 1 January 2025, of whom 63.6% were Norwegian [23][24].
